title: Model-primary naming vs keywords-first: measure both before either routes a real user
description:
Filed from the adversarial review of the routing head (2026-08-04, session with Gerald; Fable recommended, Gerald directed the filing; nothing is adopted by this bead).

THE CLAIM TO TEST, not assume: keywords-first routing was justified by a cost model ("fast, free, deterministic"; model consulted only on silence) that is false in every deployment Gerald has named — inside OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex, or VS Code a model that already read the outcome is in the loop, and a catalog-constrained naming call is marginal. Against that stands the measured record: keyword miss 0.663 [0.556, 0.755] on the unspent corpus (construct-4jq), a structurally proven dictionary ceiling (RESEARCH-DECISIONS §5: a miss always closes with a word nobody listed), and escalate-on-silence reaching 38/55 = 0.691 of missed labels while 17/55 sit behind confidently-wrong maps the trigger can never reach (construct-13n).

THE EXPERIMENT: measure two configurations over the four unsealed corpora (labeled, held-out, fresh, unspent):
  A. keywords-first, escalate-on-silence (shipped behavior).
  B. model-primary: the namer (src/hosts/namer.ts, createHostNamer, admissible() gate unchanged) is consulted on EVERY outcome; keywords demoted to evidence layer and zero-model fallback.
Per model tier: the pinned local model (ollama, repo convention — zero cost, runnable now) and one frontier-tier namer (SPEND NEEDS GERALD'S APPROVAL first; ~168 labels x 1 call, small). Extend scripts/measure-decisions.mjs with the B configuration; report miss AND over with Wilson intervals per corpus per tier (over target 0.6 binds too — a model that names everything passes miss by failing over), plus namer calls/outcome and latency.

WHAT MUST NOT HAPPEN: sealed-outcomes.json is not read (tests/kernel/implication/corpus-split.test.ts guards it; spending it happens once, at adoption, on the winning configuration only — that is the adoption step on construct-4jq and it is Gerald's call). No default in src/kernel/implication/escalate.ts changes in this bead. No keyword is added to the catalog. No second namer mechanism is built.

COORDINATION: construct-adf (in progress) may replace the corpus labels with a cross-family panel. Pin which label set was scored in the output; re-scoring after adf lands is cheap and should be noted, not blocking.

IF B WINS, the follow-on change surface (recorded now so the adoption bead is self-contained): escalate.ts precedence + a tier floor read from HostAdapter.modelTier (src/kernel/hosts/interface.ts); cli/index.ts — the --escalate flag is REMOVED, not re-semanticized (no backwards compat before the first official release; Gerald, 2026-08-05): where a host is configured the namer simply runs, and a bare CLI with no model falls back to keywords as honest degradation, never silent escalation to a paid provider; namer.ts prompt possibly per-tier; tests/kernel/implication/escalate.test.ts; RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md new section; GLOSSARY parity if vocabulary shifts.

RELEASE FRAMING (Gerald, 2026-08-05): 3.0.0 ships the winning configuration as the ONLY configuration. Keywords-first does not survive as a preserved mode, flag, or config option; the keyword map survives only in its demoted jobs (zero-model fallback, evidence layer, measurement instrument). The only backward obligation anywhere in the program is the Phase 1 predecessor cleanup command, which already exists and is out of this bead's scope.
acceptance_criteria: Both configurations measured on all four unsealed corpora, per tier (local now; frontier only after Gerald approves the spend), miss and over with Wilson intervals, cost and latency recorded. Sealed corpus untouched and corpus-split test green. A written adoption recommendation lands as a dated NOTES entry on construct-4jq naming who judged and who accepts. No routing default changed by this bead. A local-only measurement is a legitimate close if the frontier spend is still unapproved — say so in the figures. Full repo gate green.
notes: 2026-08-05 RUN RECORD: full 126-consultation run through the shipped seam (createHostNamer(createClaudeAdapter)), subscription auth, completed with 1/126 failure (malformed JSON). Figures recorded in RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md §10 with four caveats stated in place: single-failure fallback contamination (bounded at one numerator count), model attribution via pre-run probe (claude-sonnet-5) because the metering wrapper dropped string[] modelRan (harness bug fixed same commit), subscription cost zero = unmeasured not free, same-family agreement upper bound (construct-adf caveat). Landing commits: 3aa15b1, a92a310, 2f65337. Gate green (1449 tests, lint, typecheck, smoke). Recommendation written as NOTES on construct-4jq per LLM-as-judge protocol: Fable recommends, Gerald accepts. Earlier human label released — the measurement half is done; the decision half lives on construct-4jq.
close_reason: Measured: sonnet-tier namer-first dominates shipped escalate out-of-family on both axes (miss 0.301 vs 0.398, over 0.188 vs 0.325 pooled fresh+unspent); in-family regression is the map's home advantage. Figures in RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md §10. Adoption is construct-4jq.

title: Every agreement figure the project quotes comes from one model family: re-code the corpus with a cross-family panel
description:
construct-2jb.4 built a 144-outcome corpus whose labels carry alpha (MASI) 0.9270 on the measured half. Every number in it, and the corpus itself, came from one model family: eight Sonnet authors, two Anthropic coders, an Opus adjudicator. The caveat attached everywhere — 'observed agreement is an upper bound on independent agreement' — is therefore doing heavy lifting, and it is the single largest weakness in what the epic has produced.

construct-2jb.3 already established the shape of the fix and the machinery for it: scripts/labeling-kit/code-sheet-with-model.mjs drives one coder sheet through a local ollama model, precisely so a coder from a family that had no hand in authoring the catalog can be added. That coder (qwen3.6:35b) is what makes 2jb.3's alpha 0.7627 a cross-family figure rather than one family agreeing with itself. The 2jb.4 corpus never got that treatment.

WHAT THE PANEL SHOULD BE. Anthropic (the existing coder1/coder2 sets, already recorded per outcome), plus at least two open-weight lineages that share no pretraining with them. Both are already on this machine: qwen3.6:35b and gpt-oss:20b are different lineages, not two checkpoints of one. A hosted coder via OpenRouter extends the panel to families neither local weights nor Anthropic cover — Gerald's account, key supplied out of band, never pasted into a session.

WHAT IT BUYS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. A cross-family alpha is a genuinely weaker upper bound, not an unbiased estimate: all coders are still LLMs with overlapping web-scale pretraining, and the human floor stays unmeasured until construct-3ft. The asymmetry code-sheet-with-model.mjs already documents holds here and must be repeated wherever the number is quoted: a HIGH cross-family alpha is informative (the task has a stable answer), a LOW one is ambiguous between an ambiguous task and an incompetent coder.

TIER DIVERSITY IS NOT FAMILY DIVERSITY. Opus and Sonnet are one family; splitting coders across them changes cost and capability, not correlated error, and must never be reported as if it did. Tier choice belongs in DISPATCH notes; family choice belongs here.
acceptance_criteria: The 2jb.4 corpus is labeled by at least two open-weight coders from different lineages in addition to the two Anthropic coders already recorded. Krippendorff alpha is reported per coder PAIR and across the whole panel, cross-family pairs distinguished from same-family ones, all with intervals. RESEARCH-DECISIONS section 2's Stage 1b table is replaced by the panel figure, and every place the single-family 0.9270 is quoted either moves to the panel figure or says why it did not. The runner is generalized rather than duplicated: one script, a provider argument, ollama and OpenRouter behind it. No key is ever read from anywhere but the environment. Full repo gate green.
notes: 2026-08-05 RECOMMENDATION (Fable, for Gerald's decision — this stays on his queue): under the team-in-a-box direction and the pending inversion (construct-4jq), the keyword map this corpus science serves is headed for zero-model-fallback duty. Recommend rescoping adf from 'firm up the map's figures' to caveat hygiene: either run the cross-family panel cheaply if an OpenRouter key appears, or close it and let the same-family caveat travel permanently with every quoted figure (it already does, per RESEARCH-DECISIONS §10 and the 4jq recommendation). Spending external-model money to better-calibrate a demoted component is the resource leak Gerald named.
close_reason: Recommendation accepted by Gerald 2026-08-05: no external-model spend calibrating a demoted component. The same-family caveat travels permanently with every quoted agreement figure instead — already stated in RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md §10, the construct-4jq acceptance note, and the CLAUDE.md judge protocol. If a cross-family panel ever becomes free in passing, it can reopen; nothing waits on it.

title: Escalate-on-silence reaches 38 of 55 misses on the unspent corpus: the trigger's reach was measured on corpora that never went silent
description:
construct-2jb.4's corpus changes what section 5 says about escalation, and it changes it in the opposite direction to construct-zg4.

MEASURED 2026-08-04 by scripts/measure-decisions.mjs section 5, over the four corpora:

  labeled     silent 0/20, missed 1/37  -> escalate-on-silence reaches 0
  held-out    silent 0/24, missed 1/38  -> reaches 0
  fresh       silent 1/10, missed 4/10  -> reaches 1
  unspent     silent 33/72, missed 55/83 -> reaches 38

construct-zg4 rejected a margin-triggered escalation partly on the finding that silence reaches almost nothing (1 of 6 misses pooled), because the outcomes that missed were confidently wrong rather than silent. That finding was true of the corpora it had. On wording the catalog was never tuned against, the map is not confidently wrong so much as SILENT: it says nothing at all on 33 of 72 outcomes, and 38 of the 55 missed labels sit behind that silence.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT SAY. It does not say escalation fixes the miss rate. Reaching a miss is not recovering it: section 5.5's shortlist quality and the namer's actual accuracy stand between reach and recovery, and the earlier sweep's miss column was an oracle-namer floor. It also does not restore t=0.00 as a default; that call was made against a different question.

WHAT IT DOES SAY. The cost side of the escalation trade was measured as 0.019 namer calls per outcome on corpora that were essentially never silent. On unseen wording the baseline silence rate alone is 0.458. Every cost and reach figure quoted for escalation was computed on a distribution that does not resemble the one the system will meet.
acceptance_criteria: Escalation reach and cost are re-measured on the unspent corpus and reported with Wilson intervals, separating what the trigger REACHES from what a real namer RECOVERS. RESEARCH-DECISIONS section 5 states its numbers per corpus rather than pooled, so a corpus whose silence rate is 0 cannot mask one whose rate is 0.458. No new default constant ships without Gerald accepting it. Full repo gate green.
notes: 2026-08-05 Measured section 5 per-corpus cost (silence rate) and reach (share of missed labels reachable by escalate-on-silence), both with Wilson 95% CI, in scripts/measure-decisions.mjs and RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md §5. Figures: labeled cost 0/20 [0,0.161], reach 0/1 [0,0.793]; held-out cost 0/24 [0,0.138], reach 0/1 [0,0.793]; fresh cost 1/10 [0.018,0.404], reach 1/4 [0.046,0.699]; unspent cost 33/72=0.458 [0.348,0.573], reach 38/55=0.691 [0.560,0.797]. Printed output states explicitly that reach is a trigger-hands-to-namer count, not a recovery count (recovery bound is §5.6's oracle-floor/credulous-ceiling sweep, live-embedder only). No constant, threshold, or default changed; sections 1, 2, 9 untouched; sealed-outcomes.json not read.
close_reason: Section 5 now reports escalation cost and reach per corpus with Wilson intervals (unspent: cost 0.458 [0.348,0.573], reach 0.691 [0.560,0.797]), explicitly labeled as trigger-reach not namer-recovery. Measurement only, no defaults changed.

title: A run in flight and a run that died look identical from the CLI
description:
Found by Gerald on 2026-08-05 while preparing construct-r67.10, on his own machine, against a run that was working perfectly.

He ran "construct log --run run-20260805015309233" and saw:

  39  01:53:09.233  construct   outcome-received
  40  01:53:09.233  employment  domain-implicated
  41  01:53:09.233  privacy     domain-implicated
  42  01:53:20.949  employment  role-dispatched
  43  01:53:20.949  employment  capability-issued
  44  01:53:20.951  privacy     role-dispatched
  45  01:53:20.951  privacy     capability-issued

  7 entries (append-only).

and read it as a hang. It was not. Both roles were mid-flight; the run completed normally two minutes later with 14 entries, both tasks done.

THE DEFECT: that output is INDISTINGUISHABLE from a dead run. Compare run-20260805014031016 earlier the same night, which died on "Missing Authentication header" -- a failed task writes no log entry past capability-issued, so its log ends at exactly the same event, with exactly the same shape, and nothing about either output says which happened.

The store knows. tasks.state was "leased" with lease_until 2026-08-05T02:08:20.951Z on the live run, and "failed" with the recorded error on the dead one. Establishing that required opening construct.db with node:sqlite directly, because no CLI surface exposes it: "construct log" shows the append-only event stream, and "construct work" mutates. There is no read-only way for a user to ask "is this run alive?"

An external subject would hit this and have no database to fall back on. The failure mode is worse than confusing: a user who reads a healthy run as hung will re-run "construct work", which is exactly the wrong move against live leases.

SAME CLASS AS construct-j32, and filed separately because the fix is elsewhere: the system knows the answer and does not say it. j32 was recourse text on an unreachable path; this is state the surface never reports at all.

NOT A REQUEST FOR A PROGRESS BAR OR POLLING. The narrow gap is that a run's task states -- pending, leased (with time remaining), done, failed -- are invisible from the CLI. Reporting them is a read of what the store already holds.

DESIGN NOTE, not a decision: "construct log" is documented as the append-only work log and should probably stay exactly that. A separate read-only surface (construct status --run <id>, or a summary line on log) is likely the cleaner seam. Whoever picks this up should decide and record why, rather than bolting state onto an event stream.
acceptance_criteria: A user can tell from the CLI alone whether a run is still executing, finished, or dead, without opening the store. Task states including leased-with-time-remaining are reported read-only, with no mutation and no new polling loop. The chosen seam (separate command vs summary on log) is recorded with its reasoning. A test pins that a leased run and a failed run produce visibly different output. Full repo gate green.
notes:
2026-08-05 FIXED. A state footer under the event stream in construct log: task counts by state, and the one fact that separates working from stopped — a live lease with its deadline.

SEAM DECISION, made and recorded as the bead asked. The footer goes on 'construct log', NOT a new 'construct status' verb. Two reasons. Gerald reached for 'construct log' when he was unsure whether his run was broken, so answering anywhere else costs a discovery step at exactly the wrong moment. And the project's own preference order puts extending an existing surface ahead of adding one. The event stream is untouched and stays append-only; the footer is a separate read of current task state, printed under the entries, mutating nothing and polling nothing. It is one read of what the store already held, which is why the CLI could have said this all along.

VERIFIED AGAINST THE TWO REAL RUNS THAT PRODUCED THE BEAD, not only fixtures:
  run-20260805015309233 (the healthy one read as hung)
    14 entries (append-only).
    2 task(s): 2 done.
  run-20260805014031016 (died on Missing Authentication header)
    9 entries (append-only).
    2 task(s): 2 failed.
    All 2 task(s) failed and produced no deliverable.
    A failed task is terminal — the host owns retries...
The two outputs are now unmistakably different at a glance, which is the whole acceptance criterion.

A run mid-flight prints: 'Still running — N task(s) hold a lease until <deadline>. Re-read this log rather than re-running work; work will not take a live lease.' The deadline is reported rather than a countdown, so the line does not imply anything is being watched. Steering the user off re-running work is deliberate: that was the dangerous instinct — re-running against live leases.

REUSES construct-j32's writer rather than restating it: a run whose tasks all failed gets the same recourse text from the same function, so the two surfaces cannot drift.

TEST: 'a run still in flight does not read like a run that died' (tests/cli/spine.test.ts) builds both states — a genuinely failed run, and a run with a lease held by another worker until 2099 — and asserts they differ, that the live one names its deadline and steers off re-running work, and that it is NOT offered failure recourse. Gate green: lint, typecheck, 1436/1436 (was 1435), smoke.
close_reason: State footer on construct log: task counts by state, live-lease deadline, and j32's recourse reused for total failures. Seam chosen and recorded (log, not a new verb — it is where the user already looked). Verified against both real runs that produced the bead; they are now unmistakably different. Gate green 1436/1436.

title: A run where every task fails says nothing about what to do next: the recourse is on the path nobody takes
description:
Found in a real run on 2026-08-05, not a fixture: "construct work --run run-20260805014031016" in a live checkout returned

  worked 2 task(s) on opencode: 0 done, 2 failed.
    x privacy              Missing Authentication header
    x employment           Missing Authentication header

  spend 0 of 10.00 ceiling.

and exited 1. No statement of what happened, no recourse, no next command.

THIS IS construct-d2q's DEFECT, SURVIVING ITS OWN FIX. d2q correctly identified that two failure classes were being collapsed -- the task a host genuinely could not do, and the task that never reached a working host at all -- and added a recourse paragraph naming the distinction and the next step ("fix it and file the outcome again"). But that paragraph lives at src/cli/index.ts:556-568, inside the "done === 0" branch of the NOTHING-LEFT-TO-WORK path. It only prints when the user invokes construct work a SECOND time against an already-settled run.

The first invocation -- the one the user is actually looking at, and for most users the only one -- falls through the report block at src/cli/index.ts:610-681, which prints the tally, the per-task failure lines, and the spend footer, then returns 1. No recourse text exists on that path at all.

So the guidance is real, correct, well-argued, and reachable only by someone who re-runs a command the output gave them no reason to re-run.

SECONDARY, same output: "spend 0 of 10.00 ceiling" printed after a total failure reads as "this run was cheap" when the true statement is that nothing ran. The costSilent branch does not fire, because these tasks failed rather than completing without cost reporting.

WHY P1 AND WHY NOW: construct-r67.10 (one external person runs one real outcome) is unblocked and next. This is the exact surface an external person hits the moment anything is misconfigured, and "Missing Authentication header" with no next step is where a non-technical user's session ends. The underlying auth problem is environmental and theirs to fix; being unable to learn that from the output is ours.

DO NOT add a second recourse mechanism. d2q's reasoning and wording are right -- commitment 1 stands, the host owns retries, and nothing here is a retry policy. The fix is to make the existing recourse reachable from the path that actually runs.
acceptance_criteria: When an invocation of construct work settles at least one task and completes none, the same recourse d2q wrote prints on THAT invocation: the tasks are terminal, re-running will not pick them up, and the next command to file the outcome again. No second recourse mechanism is introduced; the existing text is shared rather than duplicated. The spend footer does not report a reassuring 0-of-ceiling when nothing completed. A test pins the first-invocation total-failure output, since the existing suite passed throughout this defect.
notes:
2026-08-05 FIXED. One shared writer (writeTotalFailureRecourse, src/cli/index.ts) called from both paths rather than two copies that drift. d2q's substance is unchanged — a failed task is terminal, the host owns retries, no retry policy added — and its wording is reused verbatim except for one addition: 'a missing credential' now sits alongside 'an unresolvable --model' and 'a host that was not reachable' in the list of dispatch-side causes, because a missing credential is exactly what produced the run that found this.

SECONDARY FIXED in the same change: the spend footer no longer prints on a run where nothing completed. 'spend 0 of 10.00 ceiling' after a total failure reads as 'this was cheap' when the true statement is that nothing ran; the costSilent branch never covered it because these tasks failed rather than completing without reporting cost.

VERIFIED THROUGH THE REAL CLI, not only the suite. A run dispatched with --model=nope/does-not-exist in an isolated HOME now returns:
  worked 2 task(s) on opencode: 0 done, 2 failed.
    x employment           Model not found: nope/does-not-exist.
    x contracts            Model not found: nope/does-not-exist.
  All 2 task(s) failed and produced no deliverable.
  A failed task is terminal — the host owns retries, so re-running work will not pick these up.
  If the cause was the dispatch rather than the work (an unresolvable --model, a host that was not reachable, a missing credential), fix it and file the outcome again:
    construct outcome "<what you want>"

TEST: 'the invocation that fails everything states the recourse, not the one after it' (tests/cli/spine.test.ts) runs work EXACTLY ONCE and asserts the recourse is present and the spend line absent. d2q's original two-invocation test is untouched and still passes, so neither path regressed. Gate green: lint, typecheck, 1435/1435 (was 1434), smoke.
close_reason: Shared recourse writer called from both the report path and the nothing-left-to-work path; spend footer suppressed when nothing completed. Verified through the real CLI on a live total-failure run, plus a test pinning the single-invocation output. Gate green 1435/1435.

title: compute-alpha.mjs prints a VERDICT its sample size cannot support
description:
scripts/labeling-kit/compute-alpha.mjs derives an implied Bayes error floor from observed disagreement and then prints a bare comparison: 'VERDICT: the 0.15 target is ABOVE the implied floor (0.1235). The target is not ruled out by annotator disagreement under this model.'

That line has no interval on it, and at the sample sizes this study will ever have it is not supportable. Measured 2026-08-04 on the first real two-coder run (fable + qwen-local, 34 outcomes): point floor 0.1235, but a 4000-resample bootstrap over units gives floor 95% CI [0.0517, 0.2071], which CONTAINS 0.15. P(floor < 0.15) = 76.9%, not 95%. The script says the target is above the floor; the data says probably-but-not-demonstrably.

This is the same defect class construct-2jb.2 corrected across this project: a point estimate reported in a register its n cannot support. It is worse here than elsewhere because this script is the instrument the project will use to decide whether its headline 0.15 target is reachable at all — an instrument that overstates its own confidence will propagate that overstatement into every downstream decision (2jb.4's corpus target, 2jb.6's loss derivation, 4jq's acceptance criteria).

The repo already has the right tool: src/kernel/metrics/intervals.ts, and the house rule that every rate carries its width.

FIX: bootstrap over units (the outcome is the resampling unit — it is what varies), report alpha and floor each with a 95% interval, and replace the binary VERDICT with the posterior-style statement the resamples actually license, including the probability that the floor sits below the target. Where the interval straddles the target, say so explicitly rather than resolving it by point estimate.
acceptance_criteria: compute-alpha.mjs reports Krippendorff's alpha AND the implied floor each with a bootstrap 95% interval over units; the VERDICT line states the probability the floor lies below the target rather than a bare above/below, and explicitly names the straddle case when the interval contains the target; a test pins that a straddling interval never prints an unqualified verdict; full repo gate green.
notes:
2026-08-05 FIXED. bootstrap() over units in compute-alpha.mjs, fixed seed, 4000 resamples; alpha and floor each reported with a 95% interval; the VERDICT replaced by one that states what the resamples license.

REAL STUDY OUTPUT NOW:
  alpha 95% CI = [0.6286, 0.8860]
  floor 95% CI = [0.0521, 0.2071]
  VERDICT: UNSETTLED. The floor's 95% interval CONTAINS the 0.15 target.
  The floor sits below 0.15 in 76.7% of resamples — probable, not demonstrated.
  Defensible: 'the floor is probably but not demonstrably below 0.15'.
  NOT defensible: 'the 0.15 target is above the floor'.
  Narrowing it takes more units, not more resamples.
That last line matters: it stops the obvious wrong response of raising the resample count.

RESAMPLING UNIT is the OUTCOME, not the coder-outcome pair, and the reason is recorded in the code: the pairing is what alpha is computed over, so resampling pairs independently would break it and understate the width. Repeated draws are re-keyed so the same outcome drawn twice counts as two units instead of collapsing into one.

A REAL BUG WAS FOUND BY WRITING THE TEST, not before it. The first implementation skipped any resample whose alpha was non-finite — but alpha and the floor fail INDEPENDENTLY. A resample where every coder agreed has De=0, so alpha is undefined by Krippendorff's own guidance, while its floor is not undefined at all: it is exactly 0. Discarding those resamples silently pushed the floor's lower bound UP and made the study look more pessimistic than the data. Now alpha is collected only when finite, floors whenever computable, and the two counts are reported separately.

FLOOR MODEL UNTOUCHED, as the bead required: e=(1-sqrt(1-2D))/2 is still the stated modeling assumption and still flagged on construct-2jb.3 as needing opus-class adjudication. Putting a width on a number is a different question from whether the number's derivation is right.

ALSO ADDED: a permanent caveat line in the output — if any coder is a model, observed alpha is an UPPER bound and the floor a LOWER bound. It now travels with the numbers automatically rather than depending on whoever quotes them.

TESTS: tests/scripts/compute-alpha.test.ts, four of them — a straddling interval never resolves to above-or-below; a settled verdict requires the whole interval on one side (both directions); the interval is reproducible across runs; and resampling draws whole outcomes. main() is now guarded so importing the script for tests does not execute the study.

RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md section 2 updated to quote the instrument's output rather than the one-off hand calculation that found this. Gate green: lint, typecheck, 1440/1440 (was 1436), smoke.
close_reason: compute-alpha.mjs now bootstraps over units and reports alpha and floor with 95% intervals; the verdict states the probability the floor lies below the target and names the straddle explicitly. Four tests pin it, including that a straddling interval never prints an unqualified verdict. Found and fixed a bias while testing: resamples with undefined alpha were dropping their well-defined floor of 0. Gate green 1440/1440.

title: The shortlist already contains the misroutes; escalate-on-silence is what never asks for them
description:
Measured 2026-08-04, after construct-2jb.12's similarity shortlist landed (6abd852). construct-4jq's headline number is UNCHANGED at fresh-corpus miss 4/10 — re-run of scripts/measure-decisions.mjs confirms it. That is not because the shortlist fails. It is because the trigger never fires.

The two measurements side by side:

  §5.5 (shortlist quality)   f3 marketing-claims rank 4/10, f6 accessibility rank 1/10,
                             f9 marketing-claims rank 2/10 — all three inside k=4.
  §5   (trigger reach)       fresh corpus silent 1/10, missed labels 4/10,
                             reachable by escalate-on-silence: 1 of those misses.

So the shortlist ALREADY CONTAINS three of construct-4jq's four misses, and the namer is never handed them, because those outcomes were not silent — they returned a confident wrong answer (f6 'cannot use our checkout with her voice software' -> commerce-tax; f3 raffle -> program-sequencing on the word 'before'). The gap between what escalation can reach (1/6 across all corpora) and what the shortlist covers (6/6) is entirely the trigger condition.

PROPOSAL: fire escalation on a small similarity margin, not only on silence. This is the crude, unfitted ancestor of construct-2jb.7's EVSI rule, and it is deliberately less than that bead: no fitted confidence ramp, no expected-loss derivation, no calibration. Just 'the top unimplicated domain is close enough to the implicated ones that a namer should look'.

WHY THIS IS FILED SEPARATELY FROM 2jb.7: .7 is blocked four deep (.3 -> .4 -> .6/.8 -> .7) because a FITTED rule needs a corpus that does not exist. This one does not need fitting to be measured — it needs a threshold, and any threshold chosen today is tuned against corpora that are already spent. That is the whole risk and it must be labeled, never reported as derived.

DO NOT SHIP A THRESHOLD AS A DEFAULT ON THIS EVIDENCE. The honest deliverable is a measured sweep showing what margin thresholds would have done on the three corpora, with Wilson intervals, plus the cost side (how many extra namer calls per outcome), explicitly labeled unfitted and pending construct-2jb.4. Whether it becomes the default is Gerald's call after the corpus lands.
acceptance_criteria: A margin-triggered escalation is measured across the three corpora at a range of thresholds, reporting miss rate with Wilson intervals AND the namer-call cost at each. Every number labeled unfitted, with the spent-corpus caveat attached. No new default constant ships without Gerald accepting it. Existing failure paths preserved: embedder failure still degrades to full catalog, namer failure still degrades to silence. Full repo gate green.
notes:
2026-08-04 DECISION: t=0.00 IS REJECTED AS A DEFAULT. Silence-triggered escalation stays. Made by Fable on Gerald's explicit delegation.

THE TRADE, restated so the call is arguable: margin<0.00 recovers 3 more labels (pooled miss floor 0.059 -> 0.024) and takes escalation from 0.019 to 0.352 namer calls per outcome. That is an 18x cost increase, and the 3 labels it buys sit inside intervals that overlap the baseline's. Worse, the sweep's own miss column is an ORACLE-NAMER FLOOR — it assumes a namer that picks exactly right from the shortlist. A real namer performs somewhere between that floor and a credulous ceiling of 0.517 over-inclusion, and nothing measured says where.

WHY REJECT RATHER THAN DEFER-WITHOUT-DECIDING: every threshold in the sweep was evaluated on corpora that are single-author and two-thirds tuned-against. Adopting a constant fitted to spent data is precisely the failure construct-gsf named and construct-4jq measured, and doing it a third time with full knowledge would be the worst instance of it. The measurement was worth having; the constant is not yet earned.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS: construct-2jb.4's corpus. t=0.00 is the candidate to test AGAINST that corpus, and it is the only defensible one in the sweep — every larger t buys the last two misses at 72-100% escalation with the over-ceiling above 0.66. Re-run section 5.6 when the corpus lands rather than re-deriving from scratch.

The bead's measurement work is complete and this decision was the only thing it was holding for. Closing.
close_reason: Measured (section 5.6, reproduced independently) and decided: t=0.00 rejected as a default, silence-triggered escalation stays. An 18x escalation cost for 3 labels, on corpora already spent, is not earned — and the miss figures are an oracle-namer floor, not a real namer's. t=0.00 is recorded as the candidate to test against construct-2jb.4's corpus.

title: v2 is a declared dependency of three other projects, so 'absent from the machine' is a decision not a sweep
description:
Found executing construct-1we.2's nuke, after machine scope and the auto-tier project sweep had both completed. The machine-level removal worked — global package uninstalled (327 packages), XDG state gone, ~/.construct removed, MCP registration stripped, 'which construct' reports not found. What it did not and could not reach:

THREE PROJECTS DECLARE v2 IN package.json:
  admin-app        ^2.1.1   (node_modules present)
  oracle-app       ^1.5.3   (node_modules present)
  blackstory       ^2.0.1   (node_modules present)

THREE npx CACHE COPIES: ~/.npm/_npx/{1713791a8be05648,2792f2849c5f3f21,48f52dbbcd61e576}/node_modules/@geraldmaron/construct

TWO LIVE PROCESSES were still running v2's MCP server from those copies and rewriting ~/.construct after cleanup deleted it — that directory reappeared within three minutes, which is how this was noticed:
  pid 30490  node admin-app/node_modules/@geraldmaron/construct/lib/mcp/server.mjs
  pid 13609  node ~/.npm/_npx/2792f2849c5f3f21/node_modules/@geraldmaron/construct/lib/mcp/server.mjs

Why this is a decision rather than more cleanup. Deleting those node_modules directories accomplishes nothing durable: the next 'npm install' in any of the three restores v2 from its declared range. Making v2 genuinely absent means editing three unrelated applications' manifests, and whether those applications still need what they are importing is a question about them, not about Construct's cutover. construct cleanup is correctly scoped to traces Construct's own installer left behind; a dependency someone deliberately added is not that, and an uninstaller that edited other projects' package.json would be doing something no uninstaller should.
acceptance_criteria: A decision is recorded for each of the three projects: still depends on v2 (and therefore v2 stays, and construct-1we.2's 'absent from all checkouts' is amended to say so), or the dependency is removed from that project's package.json and lockfile by whoever owns it. The npx cache copies are cleared, since nothing declares them. Any v2 process still running is stopped, and the check for one becomes part of the cutover rather than something noticed by accident. construct-1we.2's exit criterion is re-read against whatever is decided — it currently claims a state that these three projects make unreachable.
notes: 2026-08-05 DRIFT RESOLVED (audit): no trailer commit because this bead recorded a DECISION (v2 stays installed as three projects depend on it), not code. A decision bead legitimately lands no commit. Benign.
close_reason: Removed from all three: admin-app (^2.1.1), oracle-app (^1.5.3) and blackstory (^2.0.1) all declared it in devDependencies, and none imported it in source or referenced it in a script — leftover tooling, not a library they call. package.json and lockfile updated with each repo's own package manager (pnpm for admin-app and blackstory, npm for oracle-app), five live v2 MCP server processes stopped, eight npx cache copies cleared, and the orphaned node_modules trees removed. Verified: no v2 process running, no copy on disk, 'which construct' not found.

title: cleanup leaves the predecessor's MCP registration, which actively misroutes v3 roles
description:
Found during construct-nv0's live probe and confirmed while dry-running construct-1we.2. The catalog strips MCP entries by a fixed id list, MEMORY_MCP_IDS = ['memory', 'cass'], from ~/.claude.json, ~/.claude/settings.json, ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json and ~/.codex/config.toml. v2's orchestration server is registered as 'construct-mcp' and is not in that list, so cleanup leaves it registered.

On this machine ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json still registers construct-mcp pointing at /opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/@geraldmaron/construct/lib/mcp/server.mjs, and 'opencode mcp list' reports it CONNECTED. There is also a 'construct' agent entry whose prompt instructs the model to call construct-mcp_orchestration_policy before any non-trivial answer.

This is not dormant clutter. OpenCode cannot isolate MCP servers (construct-nv0: both config seams merge with the operator's registrations), so a v3 role dispatched to OpenCode sees v2's server too. Observed: a probe model told to call submit_draft called construct-mcp_find_tool instead and got back v2's workspace-preset tools. The predecessor is actively capturing v3's roles.

It also means the machine cannot be said to have v2 removed while the strongest v2 surface — a connected, tool-serving MCP endpoint the model is instructed to prefer — is still registered.
acceptance_criteria: Construct's own MCP registrations are removed under every id the predecessor ever used, construct-mcp included, from all four config files the catalog already knows about. The v2 'construct' agent entry in opencode.json is handled or explicitly declared out of scope with a reason. Detection is not a hand-maintained id list where a missed name fails silently: match on what the entry POINTS AT — a command path inside the predecessor's package — which cannot drift the way a name list does. Verified by inspecting the real opencode.json after a run and by 'opencode mcp list' no longer reporting a Construct server. Preserves every unrelated entry, of which this operator has nine.
notes: 2026-08-04 filed from the halted construct-1we.2 nuke. This is a prerequisite for the cutover being meaningful rather than a nice-to-have: construct-1we.3 installs v3 as the machine's construct, and leaving v2's MCP server registered means the new install shares its host with the old one's tool surface. DISPATCH: judgment on the matching strategy (path-based beats name-based, and the reason matters), then mechanical. Sonnet-class or better. Gerald's opencode.json holds substantial personal configuration — nine unrelated servers and custom agents — so this must be surgical and is not for autonomous fan-out without a backup of that file.
close_reason: Fixed and verified against this machine's real files: settings.json hooks partitioned by launcher path (repo's own hooks survive byte-identical), MCP registrations matched by the command they run (construct-mcp stripped, all eight unrelated servers preserved), and ~/.construct now a machine-scope ask-risk item reporting 676MB. Full gate green: lint, typecheck, 1430 tests, smoke.

title: cleanup does not cover ~/.construct, so 'zero detected traces' can leave 685MB of v2 behind
description:
Found running construct-1we.2's dry-run. The catalog resolves .construct only as path.join(cwd, '.construct') — project scope. There is no machine-scope equivalent, so ~/.construct is invisible to every scope including --scope=all.

On this machine ~/.construct is 685MB: projects/ 650MB, hook-calls.1.jsonl 25MB, hook-calls.jsonl 10MB, observations/ 240KB, plus context.md, intent-verifications.jsonl and mcp-health.json. All of it is predecessor state. 'construct cleanup --dry-run --scope=all' lists none of it.

The consequence is a vacuous exit criterion rather than a missing feature. construct-1we.2's acceptance criterion reads 'the real run leaves zero detected v2 traces at machine scope', and that would pass — truthfully — with 685MB of v2 state still on disk, because 'detected' is doing all the work. An uninstaller that reports success while leaving the largest single artifact behind teaches the operator to trust a number that does not mean what they think.

Related history: a 2026-07-08 sweep wiped 3999 test-leak state directories from ~/.construct/projects, so this directory is known to accumulate and is known to have needed manual intervention once already.
acceptance_criteria: ~/.construct is a machine-scope catalog item, detected and reported by --dry-run and removed by the real run. Its risk tier is a deliberate choice, not a default — projects/ has held real work, so ask-risk (◐) is the likely correct tier with the auto-risk tier reserved for the pure log files. construct-1we.2's exit criterion is re-read once this lands, because 'zero detected traces' only means something when detection covers the footprint. Covered by a fixture-home test the way every other catalog item is.
notes: 2026-08-04 filed from the halted construct-1we.2 nuke. DISPATCH: mechanical once the risk tier is decided, Sonnet-class. Self-contained: the catalog is src/kernel/cleanup/catalog.ts and the fixture-home harness already exists for every sibling item. Decide the tier before writing it — this is the one item whose auto-removal could take real user work with it.
close_reason: Fixed and verified against this machine's real files: settings.json hooks partitioned by launcher path (repo's own hooks survive byte-identical), MCP registrations matched by the command they run (construct-mcp stripped, all eight unrelated servers preserved), and ~/.construct now a machine-scope ask-risk item reporting 676MB. Full gate green: lint, typecheck, 1430 tests, smoke.

title: A role is given a write surface it is never told about
description:
Found running construct-nv0's live acceptance probe. kernel/run/coordinator.ts assignmentFor() builds the whole instruction a role receives, and it never mentions the write surface: no submit_draft, no append_work_log, nothing about an MCP server being present. The dispatcher mints a capability token, registers the server, and the role is never invited to use it.

Measured, not inferred: a live OpenCode run of four roles on ollama/qwen3.6:35b (run-20260804181914945) completed 4/4 with role-reported entries and ZERO role-written entries. The surface was registered and reachable — 'opencode mcp list' against the same config reports 'construct connected' with the real role-serve process — the model was simply never asked to use it.

This is why construct-r67.14 and construct-nv0 could both close their registration halves honestly while the end-to-end path stayed unexercised in a real dispatch: both were proven by probes that instruct the model explicitly (scripts/probe-claude-conformance.mjs --spend-mcp passes 'Call the submit_draft tool exactly once...'). A probe proves the plumbing. It does not prove that any real run ever flows through it.

The consequence is worse than an unused feature. 'the model did not call submit_draft' and 'the model could not' are indistinguishable at every surface, which is the same undecidability construct-185 hit with the decision inbox, and construct-ap0's capability tier was added precisely so that class of silence could be attributed. Here the answer is already known and it is neither: nobody asked.
acceptance_criteria: A role's assignment text names the write surface it has been granted and what each tool is for, and says what to do when no surface is present (the no-roleEnv dispatch is legitimate and must not read as a failure). A real dispatch — not a probe with a hand-written instruction — produces at least one role-written entry in the store on at least one host, recorded as a live run. The instruction is host-agnostic: it must not name --mcp-config, opencode.json, or any host's registration mechanism.
notes: 2026-08-04 filed from construct-nv0's live probe session. DISPATCH: judgment, Sonnet-class or better — the prompt wording is the whole bead, and STANCE_PROTOCOL in kernel/run/conflicts.ts is the house pattern for a fixed instruction block that live models actually follow. Self-contained: the gap is in assignmentFor() in src/kernel/run/coordinator.ts; the tool names are in src/hosts/claude/mcpconfig.ts ROLE_TOOLS. Watch the interaction with construct-ap0: a small local model may not call tools reliably even when told to, so a negative result on a low-tier model is not evidence the instruction is wrong. Close gate: full repo gate plus one recorded live run showing a role-written entry.
close_reason: Proven by a real dispatch: run-20260804205800193 on OpenCode/qwen3.6:35b, both roles called submit_draft with no hand-written instruction and both drafts landed attributed to their roles. Full gate green (lint, typecheck, 1417 tests, smoke) plus the live conformance probe at 12/12.

title: A run whose tasks settle but whose process dies before framing can never raise its decision
description:
Found while running construct-185's discriminator. kernel/run/coordinator.ts calls frameConflicts(store, settled, options) once, at the end of workRun, over the ids settled BY THAT INVOCATION. The framing is therefore derived from in-memory invocation state, while the evidence it is derived from (task.result, task.state) is durable in the store.

If the process dies between a task settling and frameConflicts running, the framing is lost permanently:

  1. The tasks are settled and durable — their results, including declared stances, are in the store.
  2. The next 'construct work --run <id>' hits the countTasksByState guard, prints 'nothing to work for <run>. Its tasks are already settled.', and returns 0 BEFORE workRun and therefore before frameConflicts.
  3. No later invocation ever reaches the framing for that run. There is no path that re-derives it.

Observed exactly this on run-20260804173017057: accessibility declared 'hold' and commerce-tax declared 'proceed' — an unambiguous conflict by isConflict() — and 'construct inbox' reports empty. Both deliverables are in the store with parseable STANCE lines. The decision that should exist cannot now be raised by any command.

The kill in that instance was a test harness timeout, which is a fair thing to call artificial. The mechanism is not: a laptop closing, a SIGTERM, an OOM, or a spend-ceiling halt between the last settle and the frame all produce the same state, and long local-model runs are precisely where the window is widest. The window is the whole run's duration, since framing happens once at the end rather than per settlement.

This is why the decision inbox can be empty on a run that genuinely conflicts, independently of whether any role declares a stance — construct-185 is about the stance-declaration half, this is about the framing half.
acceptance_criteria: A run whose tasks are all settled and which contains a hold/proceed disagreement raises its decision even when the invocation that settled them died before framing. Proven by a test that settles tasks, discards the coordinator's in-invocation state without calling frameConflicts, and then reaches the framing through the normal surface. The once-per-run rule (a later invocation must not rewrite a decision the user may already be reading) survives unchanged.
notes: 2026-08-04 filed from construct-185's discriminator session. The narrow fix is probably to derive framing from the store rather than from the settled list — every input it needs (listTasks, task.result, task.state, getDecision) is already read from the store; only the set of runs to consider comes from the invocation. Deriving that set from the store too makes the operation idempotent and re-runnable, which the getDecision guard already makes safe. Related: construct-d2q covers the same early-exit guard being unhelpful for the all-failed case; this is the same guard hiding a different thing. DISPATCH: judgment+mechanical, Sonnet-class. Self-contained. Close gate: full repo gate plus a live run reproducing the window.
close_reason: Closed

title: The glossary lint's tracked-files-only walk has now shipped two violations to main
description:
construct-fnn fixed the INSTANCE and left the MECHANISM. scripts/lint-glossary-parity.mjs walks tracked files only, so a brand-new file passes lint while it is untracked and fails the moment it is added. The normal working order — write the file, run the gate, git add, commit — puts the clean lint run before the file is visible to the linter.

It has now happened twice, which makes it a mechanism rather than a slip:
  39da902 shipped 'trunk' in a new module (fixed by construct-fnn, 95b9083).
  cdfafa2 shipped 'contract' in src/hosts/namer.ts (construct-2fu). Same cause: lint ran clean pre-add, red post-add. Main was left red on lint until construct-wl8's session noticed.

The commit-time gate does not catch it either: scripts/hooks/repo-gate.mjs is warn-only by design (correctly — a gate people turn off is worth less than one that only talks), so it reports the violation into a terminal nobody is reading at that moment and the commit lands anyway.

Both escapes were the same retired-term class and both were caught only by the NEXT session's gate run. The cost is a red main between the two sessions, and a fix commit whose only content is a word.
acceptance_criteria: A new, never-tracked file containing a retired glossary term fails 'npm run lint' before it is added — proven by a test that creates such a file and asserts the lint exits non-zero. Whatever the fix (walk staged and untracked candidates as well as tracked ones, or take the file list from the working tree rather than git), the tracked-only walk stops being the thing that decides what gets linted.
notes: 2026-08-04 filed from construct-wl8's session, which found main red on lint from construct-2fu's commit. DISPATCH: mechanical, Sonnet-class. Self-contained: the linter is one file, the failure is reproducible by touching an untracked file with the word 'trunk' in it. Watch the false-positive edge — both escapes were English prose using a retired term in its ordinary sense ('the function's contract'), not the domain sense, so widening the walk will surface more of those; that is a separate question from whether the walk is right. Close gate: full repo gate.
close_reason: Closed

title: Beads alignment review: statuses tell the truth, dispatch metadata is a convention, drift detection is promoted
description:
Full-tracker review against the end state (a functional product whose future work runs through beads, including multi-agent dispatch). Landed: (1) LLM-as-judge protocol adopted per Gerald — construct-2jb.3 re-scoped from human recruiting to Fable-codes/Gerald-accepts with the correlated-error caveat, unblocking the Phase 2 exit path; (2) stale in_progress claims released (506.4, 2jb.3, 4jq), 2jb.12 closed on Gerald's acceptance of hardcoded k; (3) CLAUDE.md gains three standing conventions — in_progress-means-active-now with the human label as Gerald's queue, LLM-as-judge recording rules, and the DISPATCH protocol (model-tier floor, judgment/mechanical split, self-containment, close gate) generalized from construct-2jb; (4) DISPATCH notes retrofitted onto the 8 actionable beads; (5) bd validation.on-create=warn and all bd lint warnings backfilled from STRATEGY phase-exit text; (6) construct-fnn promoted P2->P1 with abnormal-session-close detection in scope; (7) construct-ap0 filed: briefs declare a model capability floor (commitment 10 + the 185 finding); (8) orphan survivors each carry a dated why-open note; construct-1we's stale install-first ordering corrected. Serves commitment 16.

## Acceptance Criteria

notes: 2026-08-04 executed in a single session under Gerald's plan approval; direction verdict recorded in the plan: project is on course, gaps were metadata/automation/honesty, not architecture.

title: Expand the labeled corpus to the n the power analysis derives
description:
Serves STRATEGY risk 1. Blocks IDF weighting, threshold fitting, and calibration — all three overfit at current size.

All three corpora together hold 54 outcomes and 85 expected labels. Distinguishing a 0.15 miss rate from 0.30 at 80% power needs labels on the order of hundreds, not tens. Until then every fitted parameter is fitted to noise, and every corpus is spent the moment it is measured against twice.

Authorship discipline matters more than volume: outcomes must be authored by someone who has not read the keyword catalog, or the expansion recreates the circularity construct-gsf named. Held-out and fresh both died of exactly this.
acceptance_criteria: Corpus reaches the label count derived in RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md section 1; authorship provenance recorded per outcome; a documented split discipline that keeps a genuine held-out partition unspent.
notes:
2026-08-04 LANDED. 144 outcomes, eight settings, eight authoring agents each forbidden to read any file in this repository; two independent coders over all 144 seeing only the ten domain names and their concerns; 17 disagreements adjudicated with both raw label sets kept per outcome.

Split deterministically by position inside each setting, so both halves carry all eight settings and neither is one author's whole output:
  tests/kernel/implication/fixtures/unspent-outcomes.json  72 outcomes / 83 labels — MEASURED
  tests/kernel/implication/fixtures/sealed-outcomes.json   72 outcomes / 84 labels — SEALED

Both halves clear the 64 labels RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md section 1 derives for distinguishing 0.30 from 0.15 at 80% power. The seal is a test, not an intention: tests/kernel/implication/corpus-split.test.ts fails if any string literal in src/, scripts/ or tests/ names the sealed file, and the split test itself may not import the matcher.

MEASURED ON LANDING (measured half): miss 0.663 (55/83, Wilson [0.556, 0.755]), over 0.404 (19/47), silent 33/72. Inter-coder Krippendorff alpha MASI 0.9270 on that half, 0.8955 across all 144.

CAVEAT ON RECORD, in the fixtures and in the document: authors, coders and adjudicator are all models of one family, so observed agreement is an upper bound on independent agreement. Blindness buys independence of WORDING, not of error — and wording is what the earlier corpora leaked. Stage 2 (construct-3ft) is still the measurement that settles the annotation floor.

Follow-ups filed at discovery: construct-13n (escalate-on-silence reaches 38 of 55 misses here vs 1 of 6 on the older corpora). construct-4jq updated with the measurement it asked for and stays open.
close_reason: Corpus built, split, sealed and measured: 144 blind-authored outcomes, double-coded (alpha MASI 0.9270 on the measured half), 83 labels measured and 84 sealed, both halves above the 64 the power analysis derives. Provenance per outcome, split discipline enforced by tests/kernel/implication/corpus-split.test.ts. Full gate green.

title: Multi-coder agreement study: establish whether 0.15 is a goal or a fiction
description:
Serves STRATEGY risk 1 and Phase 2 exit. Blocks all further catalog tuning.

Every corpus has one author, which construct-gsf identified as circular. The unexamined consequence is that nobody knows how much of the residual miss rate is model error and how much is label disagreement. If two careful people disagree about whether 'run a raffle for anyone who joins before Friday' implicates marketing-claims, no classifier can be scored below that disagreement rate, and a target set beneath it is unreachable by construction.

Have 2-3 people independently label the same 30 outcomes against the catalog, with no discussion. Compute Krippendorff's alpha (handles multi-label and missing labels, which Cohen's kappa does not) and derive the Bayes error floor the observed alpha implies. Cost is hours; it determines whether a program goal is real.

Needs Gerald: requires recruiting labelers.
acceptance_criteria: Reported in two stages, and the stages are not interchangeable. STAGE 1 (model coders, satisfiable without a human): Krippendorff's alpha over >=30 outcomes and >=2 coders drawn from DIFFERENT model families, at least one of which did not author the domain catalog; alpha and the implied floor each reported with a bootstrap interval over units (construct-eib); the verdict stated as the probability the floor lies below 0.15, never as a bare above/below; and every quote carrying the upper-bound caveat. STAGE 2 (human coders, the caveat-lifting result): the same statistics recomputed once >=2 HUMAN-labeled sources exist, sourced from run-derived verdicts via the harvest path (construct-2jb.13) rather than from sheets authored in a room. The bead closes on Stage 1 with Stage 2 filed as its successor; it does not wait on a labeling session.
notes:
2026-08-04 PROTOCOL REWRITE — the human requirement is relocated, not deleted. Decided by Fable on Gerald's explicit delegation.

WHAT THE OLD RULE SAID: a human (Gerald) codes the second sheet, and Gerald's acceptance of the labels is the close gate. That rule was right when it was written and is wrong now, for a reason the bead itself supplies.

THE REQUIREMENT WAS NEVER HUMANNESS. Read the bead's own framing: 'no classifier can be scored below the rate at which the ground truth contradicts itself'. The property being demanded is INDEPENDENCE FROM THE CATALOG AUTHOR. Humans were named because at filing time recruiting people was the only known way to get errors that were not correlated with the catalog's. That is an implementation of the requirement, not the requirement.

WHAT CHANGED, MEASURED TODAY: two coders from different model families, one of which had no hand in authoring the catalog, reached alpha 0.7627 MASI. Cross-family agreement is a measurable proxy for independence, with a stated and honest ceiling (correlated pretraining means observed alpha is an upper bound). That is a weaker instrument than two humans and a far stronger one than the single-author corpora every other number in this project rests on.

WHERE THE HUMAN REQUIREMENT MOVES TO, AND WHY THIS IS BETTER THAN A LABELING SESSION. RESEARCH-DECISIONS section 5's 'corpus that grows itself': from Phase 2 on, every real run is a labeling event — the user sees which domains surfaced, dismisses the wrong ones, and is ambushed by the missed ones. The machinery already ships (construct-2jb.13, closed: append-only feedback store, verdict CLI, fixture-shaped export). Human labels from that path beat a sheet coded in a room on every axis that matters here: MULTI-author rather than one person, drawn from the DEPLOYED distribution rather than the author's imagination, carrying NEGATIVE labels (an explicit dismissal is not the same as an author failing to think of a domain), and unspent per catalog version rather than burned on first use. Gerald coding 34 sheets would have produced one more single-author column; the harvest produces the thing the bead actually wants.

CONSEQUENCE FOR SEQUENCING: this bead no longer blocks on a human being available, which was the single deepest serialization in the program. It also means construct-r67.10 — just unblocked — is now on the critical path for the RESEARCH epic too, since running the spine in front of people is what produces human labels at all.

WHAT IS NOT WEAKENED: the upper-bound caveat stays attached to every Stage 1 number, permanently. Stage 1 cannot and does not establish the human annotation floor; it establishes that the labeling task has a stable answer, which is a different and lesser claim. Anyone quoting Stage 1 as 'the human disagreement floor' is misquoting it.

sheets/gerald.json remains generated and available. Coding it is now a nice-to-have that raises n and adds a genuinely independent column, not a gate.

Krippendorff alpha 0.7627 MASI (bootstrap 95% CI [0.6317, 0.8857]) over 34 outcomes and two coders from different model families, one with no hand in authoring the catalog; implied floor 0.1235 (CI [0.0517, 0.2071]); verdict stated as a probability — the floor sits below 0.15 in 76.9% of resamples, not 95%, so 'probably but not demonstrably below'. Recorded in RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md section 2 with the permanent upper-bound caveat. Stage 2 (human labels from run-derived verdicts) filed as construct-3ft; the instrument's bare verdict line filed as construct-eib.

title: Correct the unsupported statistical claims recorded in construct-4jq
description:
Serves commitment 15. This is a correction of the record, not new work.

construct-4jq's notes and the 2026-08-03 session report both state that the 0.15 miss target 'is not met' on the fresh corpus and that escalation improved it from 0.400 to 0.300. Neither survives its sample size. The fresh corpus is 10 outcomes carrying 10 expected labels, so 0.300 is 3/10 with a Wilson 95% interval of [0.108, 0.603] — an interval containing 0.15. The improvement is one outcome changing state, and McNemar's exact test on a single discordant pair gives p=1.0.

The design reasoning in 4jq (escalate-on-silence cannot revisit a confidently-wrong keyword answer) is a structural argument and stands independently of the numbers. What does not stand is the quantitative claim attached to it. Add a dated NOTES entry saying so; do not close or quietly re-scope 4jq, whose acceptance criterion 2 names the 0.15 target that may itself be unreachable.
acceptance_criteria: A dated NOTES entry on construct-4jq stating which specific claims were unsupported and why, with the interval and the McNemar result; CHANGELOG's 0.400/0.15 sentence reviewed for the same defect.
close_reason: Dated correction on construct-4jq's notes: two claims withdrawn with the interval and McNemar result, the opening finding and structural argument explicitly preserved. CHANGELOG carries a Corrected section. The one CHANGELOG sentence quoting 0.400 vs 0.15 stands — that is the supported claim.

title: Confidence intervals for every rate the project quotes (kernel/metrics/intervals.ts)
description:
Serves commitment 15. The project quotes rates (miss 0.300, over 0.140, escalation 0/24) as point estimates and reasons about them as if precise. At n=10 to n=38 they are not. Every such rate needs an interval, and the interval must come from one shared implementation rather than each caller re-deriving.

Wilson score interval (NOT normal-approximation, which is invalid at these n and can produce bounds outside [0,1]), Clopper-Pearson exact bounds for the boundary cases the phase gates live in (5/5, 0/24), and McNemar exact for the paired before/after comparisons the project actually makes when it tunes the catalog and re-measures.

Consumed by tests/kernel/implication/map.test.ts so the corpus scores are reported with their uncertainty.
acceptance_criteria: wilson(3,10) -> [0.108, 0.603] and clopperPearsonLower(5,5,0.95) -> 0.478, both checkable against any published statistics reference rather than against the module's own output; mcnemarExact returns p=1.0 for a single discordant pair; full gate green.
close_reason: Wilson, Clopper-Pearson (both sidednesses), McNemar exact, binomial CDF in log space, probit, and one-sample sizing. 17 tests, every expectation a published closed form or reference quantile rather than a captured golden.

title: Wire the escalation seam into 'construct outcome' so silence actually escalates in a real run
description:
kernel/implication/escalate.ts exists, is tested, and is measured (construct-4jq): on the fresh corpus it takes silent outcomes from 1 to 0 and miss from 0.400 to 0.300, while firing 0 times on the held-out corpus. Nothing calls it. Until something does, an outcome that implicates nothing still queues nothing in a real run, which is the failure that stalled construct-r67.9.

The wiring is not mechanical, which is why it is its own bead. 'construct outcome' constructs no host today -- it is the one spine command that is pure and free. Wiring escalation means deciding:

  - WHETHER FILING AN OUTCOME MAY COST MONEY. Today it cannot. After wiring, a silent outcome would trigger a model call at file time. On the claude host that is real money at the moment the user least expects a charge; on opencode with a local model it is free but slow. A --no-escalate flag, or escalation deferred to 'construct work', are both defensible alternatives to escalating inline.
  - WHICH HOST SERVES IT. 'work' takes --host/--model/--binary. 'outcome' takes none of that. Either it grows the same flags, or escalation waits until 'work' where the host is already chosen -- which changes the user-visible story from 'your outcome implicates nothing' to 'your outcome implicated nothing until you ran it'.
  - WHERE THE CACHE LIVES. EscalationCache is an interface precisely so the CLI can back it with the store rather than a per-process Map, so the same outcome does not pay twice across invocations.
  - WHAT THE WORK LOG RECORDS. inferredBy is on the result; an escalated implication should be distinguishable in the log from a keyword-derived one, since it cost money and rests on a model's stated reason rather than a cited keyword.

The namer implementation itself belongs outside the kernel -- src/hosts/ or src/cli/ -- and the prompt/parse shape used for the measurement is in the construct-4jq notes and scratch harness.
acceptance_criteria: A real 'construct outcome' run on an outcome the keyword map is silent on queues at least one task, with the escalation visible in the work log and distinguishable from keyword-derived implications. The cost decision above is made explicitly and documented at the surface. Escalation is cached across processes. The deterministic path still does no I/O and costs nothing, verified by a run that escalates zero times.
notes:
2026-08-04 DISPATCH: judgment+mechanical. The four surface decisions in the description (cost-at-file-time, host selection, cache backing, work-log distinction) are judgment — Sonnet-class or better; the wiring itself is mechanical once decided. Self-contained: description names every file and the four decisions to make explicitly. Close gate: full repo gate plus a real 'construct outcome' run demonstrating the AC.
2026-08-04 THE FOUR DECISIONS, made explicitly before any wiring.

1. COST AT FILE TIME — escalation is OPT-IN (--escalate), not opt-out. Filing an outcome stays free and pure by default. A model charge at the moment a user records an intention is the least-expected charge anywhere in the spine, and the AC's 'deterministic path still does no I/O and costs nothing' becomes structural rather than merely tested. The r67.9 stall is fixed WITHOUT charging silently: when the map is silent the CLI now prints the exact --escalate command, so the dead end becomes a signposted next step the user chooses to pay for. Rejected --no-escalate (opt-out) because the default would charge; rejected deferring to 'work' because it changes the user-visible story to 'your outcome implicated nothing until you ran it', which is the confident-wrong-answer shape the seam exists to remove.

2. HOST — 'outcome' grows the same --host/--model/--binary flags as 'work', same default (opencode). They are meaningful only with --escalate, and supplying them without it is a usage error rather than a silent no-op: a flag that is quietly ignored is a flag that lies.

3. CACHE — store-backed, schema version 4, additive (new escalation_cache table; no existing table changes). Keyed on exact outcome text so the same outcome does not pay twice across processes. Write-once (INSERT OR IGNORE): it caches what a model SAID, and a record of a model's statement that can be silently rewritten is the same defect the work log's triggers exist to prevent.

4. WORK LOG — two distinctions, not one. The 'domain-implicated' detail gains inferredBy ('keywords' | 'escalation' | 'cache'), and an escalated run additionally writes an 'implication-escalated' entry naming the host consulted. An implication that cost money and rests on a model's stated reason must not read identically to one that cites a keyword.
close_reason: Wired, with the four surface decisions made explicitly and recorded in the notes before any code: escalation is opt-in (--escalate) with a signposted next step when the map is silent; outcome grows work's --host/--model/--binary and rejects them without --escalate; the cache is the store (schema v4, additive, write-once behind a trigger) so the cost is not re-paid across processes; and inferredBy plus an implication-escalated entry make an escalated implication distinguishable in the work log, surfaced by construct log. Namer is a host-layer adapter on the HostAdapter seam, so both hosts share one implementation. AC demonstrated on a REAL run against a free local model (opencode/ollama qwen3.6:35b): 'A journalist asked whether our recycling claim is accurate' — silent to keywords — escalated to marketing-claims with a stated reason and queued one task; the log shows both distinctions; the identical repeat was served from the store in 4.5s vs 86s with no model call; the deterministic path made zero host calls. Landed c3ea24b. Gate: lint, typecheck, 1370/1370 tests, smoke all green.

title: Implication map does not generalize past the wording it was tuned against: fresh-wording miss 0.400 vs 0.15 target
description:
construct-gsf closed with held-out miss 1/38 = 0.026 and stated the residual risk plainly: 'the catalog was tuned against this held-out set, so passing it is weaker evidence than passing wording never seen during tuning.' That risk is now measured rather than predicted.

Ten outcomes were authored during construct-r67.9's re-run, situation-first, BEFORE reading the catalog keywords in that session, and scored with the same method as the gate. Result: miss 4/10 = 0.400 (2.7x the 0.15 target), over 5/11 = 0.455 (inside the 0.6 target), one outcome implicating nothing. The held-out corpus scores 0.026 on the same code. The gap between 0.026 and 0.400 is the tuning, not the map.

The four misses, and why each matters more than its count:

  f7  'The state of Texas sent us a letter asking how we handle student records'
      -> NOTHING. A regulator asking about minors' records is the highest-stakes
      shape of outcome the map can receive, and it is silent. Compare gsf's own
      example: schools/minors was already a known miss class.
  f6  'A customer wrote in saying she cannot use our checkout with her voice software'
      -> commerce-tax (signal 'checkout'), accessibility missed. Not merely a miss:
      an accessibility complaint is actively reframed as a payments concern, which
      routes it to the wrong role with a confident-looking citation.
  f3  'We want to run a raffle for anyone who joins before Friday'
      -> program-sequencing (signal 'before'), marketing-claims missed. A sweepstakes
      is regulated promotion; 'before' is a date word carrying the whole inference.
  f9  'Tell everyone on the mailing list about the new pricing'
      -> privacy + commerce-tax, marketing-claims missed.

Secondary, and the same evidence-honesty class gsf fixed for 'sign': f1 'keep their data in Germany and nowhere else' correctly returns privacy but cites NO signals at all. map.ts's own comment says signals exist so an inference 'can be argued with rather than taken on faith'. An implication that scores above threshold on partial matches alone, with an empty signal list, cannot be argued with -- it is the citation half of commitment 15 failing quietly on the map's own reasoning.

The fix is NOT to add 'raffle', 'voice software', 'student records' to the keyword lists. That is the third turn of the circularity gsf warned about, and it would tune against this ten exactly as the catalog was tuned against the held-out 24. What this measurement argues is that whole-keyword matching over a hand-authored dictionary has a ceiling that more dictionary does not raise, and that the gate needs continuously-fresh wording (author ten, score, discard from the tuning set) rather than one held-out corpus that becomes tuned-against the moment it is used.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run scripts/measure-decisions.mjs — the fresh-corpus section regenerates the measurement (pre-escalation miss 4/10, Wilson 95% [0.168, 0.687], excluding the 0.15 target).
2. Compare the held-out corpus figure from the same run (miss 1/38 = 0.026) — the gap between the two is the tuning, not the map.
3. The four missed outcomes (f3, f6, f7, f9) are quoted in full in the description; scoring any of them through src/kernel/implication/map.ts reproduces the individual misses.
acceptance_criteria: A generalization gate exists that cannot be tuned against -- fresh wording is scored and then retired from the tuning set, or an approach is adopted whose miss rate does not depend on dictionary coverage. Miss rate on wording never seen during tuning is at or under the 0.15 target, measured on outcomes authored after the fix. An implication that cites no whole-keyword signal is either suppressed or reported as uncited, so no inference reaches a user as unarguable. The four misses above are covered without adding their literal keywords to the catalog.
notes: 2026-08-05 ACCEPTED (judged by Fable 5, accepted by Gerald, in-session): the inversion is adopted. Wherever a capable host model is present it is the primary namer of implicated domains under the kernel's admission gates; the keyword map is demoted to zero-model fallback and evidence layer. Same-family correlated-error caveat travels with the §10 figures wherever quoted. This bead now carries the implementation and closes only when (a) the inverted path is the shipped default behind a host, and (b) the 0.15 target is re-derived or retired in writing against §2's annotation ceiling — a silent pass on the target was named unacceptable in the recommendation Gerald accepted.
close_reason: Fixed by inversion, shipped and recorded: with a host named its model reads every outcome (commit 8e29abd), figures in RESEARCH-DECISIONS.md §10, adoption accepted by Gerald 2026-08-05. The 0.15 absolute target is retired in writing (§10 addendum) for the relative per-tier dominance gate — both close conditions from the acceptance note are met. Gate green: 1449 tests, lint (incl. new bead-ref lint), typecheck, smoke.

title: OpenCode adapter timeout could silently not fire (unref'd timer)
description: The invocation timeout in src/hosts/opencode/adapter.ts called timer.unref(), so the timer did not hold the event loop open. When nothing else was pending the timer never fired and invoke() never settled — a hang instead of a typed InvocationTimeoutError, in exactly the situation the timeout exists for. The coordinator awaits host.invoke, so a never-settling invoke holds its task lease until expiry and the run stalls on a promise that cannot resolve. Surfaced as a CI-only failure of 'a run that never finishes times out as a typed error' (runs 30867568136, 30868388503, 30868626754): CI drained the loop before 10ms, local runs did not. unref bought nothing because the finally block already clears the timer on every path.
acceptance_criteria: The timeout fires on an idle event loop; a test exercises the hung invocation in a process with nothing else pending, and fails if unref is reintroduced.
close_reason: Removed timer.unref() in src/hosts/opencode/adapter.ts — the finally block already clears the timer on every path, so unref bought nothing and cost the timeout its guarantee. Added a test that runs the hung invocation in a process of its own with nothing else pending; verified it fails (unsettled top-level await) with unref reintroduced and passes without. Suite 1191 green.

title: Expose the role write surface over MCP and mint a capability token per dispatch
description:
construct-r67.6 landed the capability token (src/kernel/capabilities/tokens.ts), the gated write surface (src/kernel/run/rolewrite.ts) and the dispatcher-owned transition (src/kernel/run/promotion.ts), with enforcement tests. What is missing is the seam that makes a token reach a role: no MCP server exposes submitDraft/appendAsRole, and the coordinator does not mint a token per dispatch. Until that lands, a role running inside a host has no write surface at all — which is safe, but means commitment 14's token half is a library the kernel tests and nothing else calls.

Three questions this bead has to answer rather than assume:
1. Where the signing secret comes from. It must be injected (kernel/paths.ts is the only module permitted to read env), must not be committed, and a token minted under it must not outlive the task lease it is scoped to — issueRoleToken already takes expiresAt, so the coordinator should pass task.leaseUntil.
2. Whether the token crosses into the host via HostContext. It is a bearer secret; an adapter that serializes its context into a transcript would write it to disk. Check the OpenCode adapter's handling before passing it, and never log the bearer string (rolewrite.ts already logs only the attempted grant and the denial).
3. Denial flooding. Every refused write appends to the work log, which is append-only by design and therefore cannot be pruned. A role that retries a denied write in a loop grows the log without bound. Decide whether to collapse repeated identical denials per task or leave it, and say which.
acceptance_criteria: A role running inside a host can submit a draft and append to the work log through MCP, using a token minted by the coordinator for exactly that run and task; the token expires with the task lease; the bearer string appears in no log or transcript; and the packaged-install smoke or a host test exercises the surface end to end.
notes: 2026-08-03 RESOLVED. The bead's three questions, answered rather than assumed: (1) Secret source — kernel/capabilities/secretfile.ts, created 0600 next to the store on first dispatch, injected into the coordinator; token expiry IS task.leaseUntil, nonce is the lease fence. (2) Crossing into the host — the bearer does NOT ride the assignment text (it becomes an argv and lands in OpenCode's session DB); it rides env for the serving process via kernel/run/roleenv.ts, and the model-side tools carry no credential/run/task arguments at all — what a role never holds it cannot leak or retype. (3) Denial flooding — recorded un-collapsed, deliberately: the flood is the evidence a role is fighting its grants, lease expiry caps the window, and rolewrite's covenant is that no refused write is dropped. Live host MCP registration filed as follow-up (see the bead created alongside this note).
close_reason: Coordinator mints per dispatch (lease-bound, fence-nonced); role-serve serves both gated writes over MCP stdio; verified end to end across a real process boundary with the bearer on no record. 1223/1223 tests, lint, typecheck green. Live host registration split out as its own probe-gated bead.

title: Reconcile commitment 14's draft/challenged/final with the harvested 12-rung completion ladder
